content: The study design included details on the intervention or follow-up, the method of randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of patients, treatment administrators, and outcome assessors. Interventions or exposures were described, including the use of placebo or comparison groups, the dose, route, and timing of interventions, co-medications, potassium intake at baseline and follow-up, and the method used to evaluate potassium intake. Participants were selected using specific sampling and randomization methods, with inclusion and exclusion criteria clearly defined. The total number of participants, their distribution across comparison groups, sex, age, baseline characteristics, diagnostic criteria, and the similarity of groups at baseline (including comorbidities) were assessed. Compliance, withdrawals, and losses to follow-up were documented, along with reasons and descriptions. Subgroups analyzed in the original study were noted, as well as the status of blood pressure and medication use for blood pressure control. Outcomes were specified, including those predefined and any additional outcomes assessed. The length of follow-up and the quality and completeness of outcome reporting were evaluated. Results were reported with the timing of assessments and measures of variation, converted to effect measures when necessary, and analyzed using an intention-to-treat (ITT) approach. The stated objective of the study was clearly defined. In cases of duplicate publications or companion references of a primary study, all available data were evaluated simultaneously to maximize information yield. The risk of bias in included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions guidelines. Sequence generation methods were described in sufficient detail to assess whether they produced comparable groups. Allocation concealment methods were categorized as adequate, inadequate, not used, or unclear. Blinding methods for participants, personnel, and outcome assessors were described and judged for adequacy. Incomplete outcome data were evaluated for attrition bias, with methods categorized as adequate, inadequate, or unclear. Selective reporting bias was assessed by determining whether all prespecified outcomes and expected outcomes of interest were reported. The selection of study participants was recorded, including how treatment and control groups were formed and whether participants were representative of the wider population. Exposure definitions and outcome data collection methods were documented, including adherence to interventions and the adequacy of follow-up length. Analytical comparability was assessed by recording steps taken to adjust for variations in treatment and control groups or exposed and unexposed groups. Other sources of bias, such as baseline group similarity, were noted. Continuous variables were expressed as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Data synthesis was performed statistically when data were available, sufficiently similar, and of adequate quality, following Cochrane Handbook guidelines. Heterogeneity was examined using the I² statistic, with substantial heterogeneity prompting narrative summaries rather than pooled meta-analytical estimates. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the effects of removing studies at high risk of bias. Studies were considered high risk if they were inadequate in randomization, allocation concealment, and either blinding or loss to follow-up. Non-randomized trials were considered high risk by default. The quality of the body of evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology. Funnel plots were planned to evaluate the potential existence of small study effects. The search process identified a systematic review on the effect of potassium on blood pressure in adults but no reviews on its effects in children. A total of 4885 references were identified, with most excluded based on title or abstract. Only one study met the inclusion criteria after full review. Additional searches identified 17 references, of which two studies met the inclusion criteria. These studies had previously been excluded due to short duration or non-random allocation. The included studies were conducted in the United States and the Netherlands. Participants were recruited through schools, churches, advertisements, or existing panels. The cohort study followed participants for seven years. The two RCTs included 250 participants, while the non-randomized trial included 76 participants. The cohort study measured 596 children at baseline, with 233 completing the evaluation. Interventions included dietary education, behavioral skills training, feedback, and potassium or placebo supplements. Outcomes measured included resting and ambulatory blood pressure, rate of blood pressure change over time, and changes in resting blood pressure over a seven-year follow-up. Results from the observational cohort study suggested a beneficial effect of increased potassium intake on blood pressure in children, though quantitative results were not provided.
